title: Tests for ions; Reactivity series and displacement
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT07#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX09#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT07#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX09#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PT07#N.6, RX09#N.2, PT07#N.12, RX09#N.6, PT07#N.14b, RX09#N.8.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cation
items.clue: The positive particle in a salt, such as Ba²⁺.

items.label: Oxidising agent
items.clue: Role of halogens, which react by gaining electrons: X₂ + 2e⁻ → 2X⁻.

items.label: Limewater
items.clue: Turns milky when CO₂ from a carbonate and dilute acid is bubbled in.

items.label: Reducing agent
items.clue: Role of metals, which react by losing electrons, as Zn does with Cu²⁺.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relative ease of reduction of the halogens is correct?

options.text: Iodine is reduced more readily than bromine, as it is further down the group.
Bromine is reduced more readily than chlorine, as its nucleus has more protons.
Iodide ions are reduced more readily than iodine, as they are charged.
Chlorine is reduced more readily than bromine, as its atoms are smaller.

questions.explanation: An electron added to a chlorine atom is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it is held more strongly.

questions.stem: A white solid gives a brick-red flame. Its solution fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. What is the solid?

options.text: Calcium carbonate
Lithium carbonate
Calcium sulfate
Sodium carbonate

questions.explanation: Brick-red is Ca²⁺; fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky is CO₃²⁻.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution: Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Iodide ions are reduced, because they lose electrons.
Chlorine is the oxidising agent, and its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1.
Chlorine is oxidised, because it forms chloride ions.
Potassium ions are oxidised, because the solution turns brown.

questions.explanation: Cl₂ gains electrons from I⁻, so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: A jar of white crystals has lost its label. It could be magnesium sulfate, calcium chloride, barium chloride or sodium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is barium chloride?

options.text: A yellow-orange flame; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
A brick-red flame; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.
No flame colour and a white precipitate with NaOH(aq); dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
An apple-green flame; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.

questions.explanation: Apple green is Ba²⁺; white AgCl, from acidified silver nitrate, shows Cl⁻. Each ion has its own test.

questions.stem: A few drops of bromine water are added to a colourless solution containing both potassium chloride and potassium iodide, in excess. Cyclohexane is then added and the mixture shaken. What colour is the top layer, and why?

options.text: Pale green, because Br₂ oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂
Orange, because Br₂ reacts with neither halide and dissolves in the cyclohexane
Colourless, because Br₂ is reduced to colourless bromide ions
Violet, because Br₂ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ but cannot oxidise Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Iodine dissolves in cyclohexane, giving violet. Cl⁻ is untouched.
